name: Testing Your Code
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Write tests a team trusts with pytest and Jest or Vitest: the test pyramid, edge cases, mocks, TDD, coverage and flaky tests.

lesson.intro: On a team, nobody merges code because it looked fine on their laptop. Tests prove a change works and stop next month's change from quietly breaking it. This lesson covers what to test, how to write tests people trust, and pytest, Jest and Vitest.
objectives: Choose between unit, integration and end-to-end tests for a change
Write clear arrange-act-assert tests in pytest and Jest or Vitest
Pick edge cases and boundary values that catch real bugs
Decide when a stub, mock or fake helps and when mocking makes tests brittle
Run the red, green, refactor loop and explain what coverage proves

sections.title: Why teams test, and the test pyramid
sections.key: Tests catch regressions, make refactoring safe, document behavior and gate merges; write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a few end-to-end tests.
sections.body:
Second week: you fix a rounding bug in `apply_discount()`, click through checkout once, and merge. Two days later, customers with a 100% coupon are charged one cent. A test suite would have tried that case for you, on every change, in seconds.

Tests do four jobs on a team:

- **Catch regressions**: once a test covers a behavior, nobody breaks it silently.
- **Make change safe**: you can refactor because tests flag any change in behavior.
- **Document behavior**: `test_expired_coupon_is_rejected` says what the code promises.
- **Gate merges**: CI runs the suite on every pull request.

[[visual]]

The **test pyramid** says how many of each:

[[visual 2]]

It is a guideline; web teams often write more integration tests. Everyone agrees the inverted pyramid is bad: the **ice cream cone**, with nearly everything checked by slow E2E runs or people clicking before each release.

visual.title: Kinds of test
rows: One function or class alone: no network, database or disk
Several real pieces together, such as an API handler writing to a test database
Points at the seam between two parts
The whole running system, used like a user would: a browser driven by Playwright or Cypress
Many concurrent requests: 500 checkouts, with the slowest 5% under 300 ms

visual.title: The test pyramid

layers.label: End-to-end
layers.detail: A few, for journeys that must never break: sign up, log in, pay

layers.label: Integration
layers.detail: Some: real database, real HTTP between your parts

layers.label: Unit
layers.detail: Many: milliseconds each, one unit at a time

visual.arrowLabel: Higher: more confidence, but slower, harder to debug and flakier

sections.tip: When you pick up a ticket, find where the existing tests for that area live before you write any code. Matching the team's testing style is part of the job.
sections.pitfall: Checking the happy path once by hand and calling it done. Manual clicking does not repeat itself on the next pull request; a test does.

check.question: You changed how `format_price()` rounds cents. Which test gives the fastest, most precise feedback?
choices: An end-to-end test that buys an item in a browser
A unit test that calls format_price() with a few amounts
An integration test that hits the checkout API and database
Asking QA to try a purchase on staging
check.explanation: The change lives in one function, so a unit test runs in milliseconds and names the exact failing case. The E2E and integration tests would also catch it, but slower and with many more places to look when they fail.

sections.title: Anatomy of a good test: arrange, act, assert
sections.key: Shape each test as arrange, act, assert, check one behavior, name it after the scenario and expected result, and assert literal values worked out by hand.
sections.body:
Most tests in a well-run codebase share one three-part shape:

- **Arrange**: build the inputs and the world the code needs (objects, data, a fake clock).
- **Act**: call the one thing you are testing, usually one line.
- **Assert**: check the outcome: a return value, a raised error, a change of state.

A blank line between the parts makes a test readable at a glance.

[[code]]

**Names matter most in tests**: a failing test's name is the first thing you read in the CI log. State the scenario and the expected result.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Test **one behavior per test**: a test stops at its first failed assert, hiding the rest. And keep logic out of tests: if the expected value reuses the code's formula, it agrees with a buggy formula. Write the literal answer: `assert total == 90.00`.

items.title: Useless when it fails
points: `test_cart_2`
`it('works')`

items.title: Says what broke
points: `test_cart_total_applies_ten_percent_coupon`
`it('rejects an expired coupon')`

visual.title: Good tests are FIRST
rows: Unit tests take milliseconds, so people actually run them
Each test sets up its own data and passes alone, with the others, and in any order
Same result every run on every machine: no real date, network or randomness unless the test controls it
The test asserts; nobody reads printed output to decide
Written together with the code, not months later

sections.pitfall: Tests that lean on each other, such as test B passing only because test A created a user first. Run them alone or in another order and they fail for reasons unrelated to the code.

check.question: Which test name is most useful when it fails in CI?
choices: test_discount_3
test_discount_works
test_discount_function_in_pricing_module
test_discount_is_capped_at_fifty_percent
check.explanation: It states the scenario and the expected result, so the failure alone tells you which promise broke. The others only say where the test lives or that something, somewhere, went wrong.

sections.title: pytest and Jest or Vitest in practice
sections.key: pytest uses plain assert, pytest.raises, parametrize and fixtures; Jest and Vitest use expect with matchers, where toBe checks identity and toEqual compares contents.
sections.body:
**pytest** is the standard Python test runner. **Jest** and **Vitest** are the common JavaScript ones, and their APIs are nearly identical.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

The matchers that trip up newcomers:

[[visual 2]]

Everyday commands:

[[visual 3]]

items.title: pytest
points: Collects files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`, and functions whose names start with `test`
Plain `assert`; a failure shows the values on both sides
`with pytest.raises(ValueError):` asserts the block raises
`@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs one body over a table; each row is reported as its own test
Fixtures (`@pytest.fixture`) build setup. A test names one as a parameter and gets a fresh one per test. Built-ins: `tmp_path`, `monkeypatch`

items.title: Jest and Vitest
points: Collect files such as `price.test.js` or `price.spec.ts`
`describe` groups tests; `it` or `test` defines one
`expect(value)` plus a matcher checks the result
Vitest: `import { it, expect } from 'vitest'`; Jest provides them as globals

visual.title: Matchers
rows: Compares with `Object.is`: is it the very same object? `expect([1]).toBe([1])` fails
Compares contents recursively. Use it for objects and arrays
Needs a function to call: `expect(() => parse('x')).toThrow()`. Without the arrow, `parse` runs before `expect`, and the error escapes and crashes the test

visual.title: Commands
rows: Watch mode: reruns affected tests as you save

sections.tip: While fixing one test, run just that test (`pytest -k name`, or `it.only` in JavaScript), then the whole suite before you push. Never commit `it.only`: it silently skips every other test in the file.
sections.pitfall: Using `toBe` to compare arrays or objects. It checks identity, so `expect([1]).toBe([1])` fails. Use `toEqual` for contents.

activity.title: Fix the tests, not the code
activity.prompt: This is a Vitest-style test file with a tiny stand-in for `it` and `expect` at the top. The function is correct, but two tests are written wrong. Run it, read the FAIL messages, then fix only the two tests: one needs a different matcher and one needs to pass a function to expect. Notice that the third failure is not a failed assertion at all, it is the error escaping.

props.task: Make all three tests print PASS without changing parseTags.
props.expectOutput:
PASS splits, trims and lowercases tags
PASS ignores empty entries
PASS rejects input that is not a string

check.question: In a Jest test, `expect(getUser()).toBe({ name: 'Ana' })` fails even though getUser returns `{ name: 'Ana' }`. Why?
choices: getUser must be awaited before any matcher can run
toBe checks that both sides are the same object; toEqual compares contents
Jest cannot compare objects, so you must compare each field separately
toBe only works inside a describe block
check.explanation: toBe uses Object.is, which is true only for the very same object. getUser builds a new object, so identity fails even though the contents match. toEqual walks both objects and compares their fields.

sections.title: Edge cases and boundary values
sections.key: Bugs cluster where a decision flips: test one value per input group, plus each boundary and one step either side, and the usual edge cases such as empty and zero.
sections.body:
A ticket says users must be at least 13 to sign up. You write `if age > 13:` and test 25 and 8. Both pass, and the bug ships: a 13-year-old is rejected. You never tested the edge where the decision flips.

- **Equivalence partitioning**: split inputs into groups the code treats the same (under 13, 13 and over). One representative per group is enough.
- **Boundary value analysis**: bugs cluster where groups meet, so test at the boundary and one step either side: 12, 13, 14. Off-by-one mistakes (`>` for `>=`, `range(n)` for `range(n + 1)`) live there.

[[visual]]

Then run through the usual suspects for the input type:

[[visual 2]]

Pick the edges the code could plausibly receive. One test per realistic edge beats ten more typical values from the middle of a partition, where code is rarely wrong.

[[code]]

items.title: Typical values: 8 and 25
points: Pass with `>` and with `>=`
Cannot tell the correct code from the buggy one

items.title: Boundary values: 12, 13, 14
points: 12 is the last "no", 13 the first "yes"
`can_sign_up(13)` fails with `>`: bug caught

visual.title: The usual suspects
rows: Empty, one element, two, many, duplicates, sorted, reverse sorted
Zero, negative, one, the maximum allowed, just past it, floats like 0.1 with no exact binary form
Empty, only spaces, very long, mixed case, non-ASCII such as "José"
Midnight, the last day of a month, February 29, time zones, daylight saving changes

sections.pitfall: Testing only typical values like 25 and 8. They pass with `>` and with `>=`, so they cannot tell the correct code from the buggy one.

activity.title: Find the off-by-one
activity.prompt: Run the tests. Two fail. Use the failing test names to work out which pages are wrong, then fix the one line in paginate that computes start. Notice that the two passing tests (past the end and empty list) could not detect this bug at all.

props.task: Fix paginate so the output is: 4 of 4 tests passed

check.question: Orders of $50.00 or more get free shipping. Which set of test amounts best covers the boundary?
choices: $50.00 only
check.explanation: The decision flips at $50.00, so test the boundary itself and the closest values on each side. That catches both `>` versus `>=` mistakes and rounding errors near the threshold. Typical values far from the edge cannot.

sections.title: Test doubles: stubs, mocks and fakes
sections.key: Replace the boundaries of your system (network, email, payments, clock, randomness) with test doubles, and keep your own code real; mocking your internals makes tests brittle.
sections.body:
`place_order()` saves to Postgres and emails the customer. Unit tests should not need a database server, send real email or fail when the Wi-Fi drops. So you hand the code stand-ins for its collaborators: **test doubles**.

[[visual]]

Code that takes collaborators as parameters (**dependency injection**) is easiest to test: pass in a fake, no patching needed.

[[code]]

**When mocking hurts.** A test that mocks five collaborators and asserts the exact call sequence mirrors the implementation, so any refactor breaks it. Mock your own database layer and the real SQL never runs. Mock a library's internals and an upgrade breaks production while tests pass.

[[visual 2]]

One Python detail: `patch` replaces a name **where it is looked up**. If `billing.py` does `from emails import send_email`, patch `billing.send_email`, not `emails.send_email`.

visual.title: Test doubles
rows: Fills a required parameter; never used
A `None` logger the code never touches
A stub that also records its calls
Check afterwards what it was called with
An in-memory repository, a fake clock, a local inbox
visual.caption: In everyday speech people call all recording doubles mocks.

items.title: Double the boundary
points: Network calls and payment or email providers
The clock and randomness
Anything slow, nondeterministic or with side effects

items.title: Keep your own code real
points: Use real objects or simple fakes inside the boundary
Cover each boundary with a few integration tests that use the real thing

sections.code:
from unittest.mock import Mock

class InMemoryOrders:              # a fake: real behavior, no database
    def __init__(self):
        self.saved = []
    def save(self, order):
        self.saved.append(order)

def place_order(order, orders, mailer):
    orders.save(order)
    mailer.send(order["email"], "Thanks for your order!")

def test_place_order_saves_and_emails_customer():
    orders = InMemoryOrders()
    mailer = Mock()                 # a mock: we check how it was called

    place_order({"id": 7, "email": "ana@example.com"}, orders, mailer)

    assert orders.saved == [{"id": 7, "email": "ana@example.com"}]
    mailer.send.assert_called_once_with("ana@example.com", "Thanks for your order!")
sections.pitfall: Mocking everything inside your own code. If a refactor that keeps behavior identical breaks twenty tests, those tests check how the code works rather than what it does.

check.question: Which collaborator is the best candidate for a test double in a unit test?
choices: A pure helper that formats dates
The dataclass that holds an order's fields
The function under test itself
The HTTP client that calls a payment provider
check.explanation: The payment client crosses the system boundary: it is slow, needs the network and has real side effects. Pure helpers and plain data classes are fast and deterministic, so using the real ones keeps the test honest. Doubling the function under test means testing nothing.

sections.title: Test-driven development: red, green, refactor
sections.key: TDD is a short loop: write one failing test, write the simplest code that passes, then refactor with every test green.
sections.body:
**Test-driven development** (TDD) flips the usual order: instead of code then tests, you go round a short loop, often a few minutes per lap.

[[visual]]

A password rule (at least 8 characters and one digit), built that way:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

You never write code nobody asked for, every behavior has a test from the start, and awkward designs show up early: code that is hard to test first is usually hard to use.

TDD shines for clear inputs and outputs (parsers, pricing, validation) and for **bug fixes**: reproduce the bug as a failing test first, then fix it, and the test guards against its return.

It is a tool, not a religion: for exploratory work, spike first, then test-drive the real version.

steps.label: Red: write one small test for the next behavior
steps.detail: Run it and watch it fail: proof the test can fail and the behavior is missing

steps.label: Green: write the simplest code that passes
steps.detail: Hard-coding is fine for a moment; the next test forces a general solution

steps.label: Run all the tests and see them pass
Refactor
steps.detail: Clean up names and duplication, running the tests after each change

steps.label: Green: also require a digit
steps.work:
and any(c.isdigit()
        for c in password)

sections.pitfall: Writing a pile of tests up front and then all the code at once. The feedback in TDD comes from the short loop: one failing test, just enough code, clean up, repeat.

activity.title: Drive it with tests
activity.prompt: All the tests are written, and slugify is a stub. Work through them in order like a TDD loop: run, read the first FAIL, write the simplest code that fixes it, run again. Notice that the empty-title test already passes with the stub, which is why a test that has never failed tells you little.

props.task: Implement slugify so the output is: 4 of 4 tests passed

check.question: In TDD, why do you run a new test and watch it fail before writing the code?
choices: pytest refuses to run tests that pass the first time
It proves the test can fail and really checks the missing behavior
It measures how long the code takes to run
It makes CI record a failed build for the ticket
check.explanation: A test that passes before the code exists is not testing what you think, for example because it asserts nothing or calls the wrong function. Seeing it fail first proves it can catch the missing behavior.

sections.title: Coverage and flaky tests
sections.key: Coverage shows code no test runs but not whether tests check anything; a flaky test passes and fails on the same code and must be fixed or quarantined fast.
sections.body:
**Coverage** measures which lines (with branch coverage, which sides of each `if`) ran during the tests: `pytest --cov=myapp` with pytest-cov, `jest --coverage`, or `vitest run --coverage`.

[[visual]]

Treat the number as a smoke alarm for untested areas, not a grade. Many teams set a floor in CI (say 80%) so it does not slide, and judge test quality in review.

A **flaky test** passes and fails on the same code:

[[visual 2]]

Flaky tests are expensive: once red sometimes means nothing, people rerun until green, stop trusting the suite, and real failures slip through. Reproduce it (run it in a loop, or the suite in random order), fix the cause, and if you cannot fix it today, quarantine it with a ticket.

[[code]]

items.title: Good at
points: Finding code no test runs at all: a module at 0%, an error branch never executed

items.title: Bad at
points: Proving tests are good: a line counts as covered if it ran, even if nothing checked its result
Seeing missing code: if nobody handled negative quantities, there is no line to be uncovered

visual.title: Why tests flake
rows: `sleep(2)` and hope a background job finished; a timeout too tight for slow CI
Poll for the condition with a timeout, or run the job synchronously in tests
A global, a module-level cache or a database row left by another test
Fails after noon, on the 31st, at midnight UTC
Inject a fixed clock; control the random seed
The real network, a third-party sandbox, DNS
Fake the boundary; test it in a few integration tests

sections.pitfall: Rerunning a red build until it turns green. Fix or quarantine the flaky test, or the team learns to ignore red builds, including the real ones.

check.question: Your pull request raises coverage from 70% to 85%. What does that prove?
choices: The newly covered lines contain no bugs
Every branch of every if statement is now tested
More lines ran during the tests, not that their results were checked
The suite is now 85% likely to catch a regression
check.explanation: Coverage records execution, not verification. A test with no asserts raises coverage just as much as a careful one. It is useful for finding untested code, not for grading the tests you have.

keyTerms.definition: A test of one function or class in isolation, with no network, database or disk. Runs in milliseconds.
A test that checks several real components working together, such as an API handler and a test database.
A test that drives the whole running app the way a user would, usually through a browser.
The guideline to write many unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few end-to-end tests.
The three-part shape of a test: set up the inputs, perform one action, check the outcome.
Behavior that used to work and broke after a change. A regression test keeps it from breaking again.
An input at the edge where behavior changes, tested together with its nearest neighbors on each side.
A stand-in for a real collaborator in a test: a dummy, stub, spy, mock or fake.
A double that records calls so the test can verify them, such as send being called once with an address.
A working, lightweight implementation used in tests, such as an in-memory repository or a fake clock.
Writing a failing test first, then the simplest code to pass it, then refactoring: red, green, refactor.
A test that passes and fails on the same code because of timing, shared state, clocks, randomness or external services.

summary: Tests catch regressions, make refactoring safe, document behavior and gate merges.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few E2E tests for critical journeys.
Arrange, act, assert; one behavior per test; names that state scenario and result.
Test boundaries and edges: empty, zero, None and the value where a rule flips.
Put test doubles at system boundaries; mocking your own internals makes tests brittle.
TDD is red, green, refactor. Coverage finds untested code, not good tests; fix flaky tests fast.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why the team wants tests with every pull request, what makes one test better than another, and how they should decide between a mock and a real object.

questions.question: Name the four jobs an automated test suite does for a team.
questions.answer: It catches regressions, makes refactoring safe, documents how the code is meant to behave, and gates merges because CI runs it on every pull request.
questions.explanation: These are the reasons teams ask for tests with every pull request. Manual checking does none of them repeatably.

questions.question: Match each kind of test to an example of it.

pairs.right: Call parse_date('2026-02-30') and check it raises ValueError
POST to /signup and check a row appears in the test database
A browser fills in the signup form and lands on the welcome page
Send 500 concurrent checkouts and check the slowest 5% stay under 300 ms

questions.explanation: Unit tests exercise one function alone. Integration tests check real components together, such as a handler and a database. End-to-end tests drive the whole app like a user. Load tests check behavior under heavy traffic rather than correctness of one case.

questions.question: Which of these are signs of an inverted test pyramid (the ice cream cone)?
choices: Before each release, people click through staging to check most features
The CI run takes 90 minutes, mostly browser tests
Hundreds of unit tests run in under a minute
When a test fails, finding the broken line takes hours
A few end-to-end tests cover login and checkout
questions.explanation: The cone is top-heavy: manual and E2E checks do the bulk of the work, so runs are slow and failures are hard to locate. A fast unit layer and a few E2E tests for critical journeys are exactly what a healthy pyramid looks like.

questions.question: Your team has 40 end-to-end tests (25 minutes) and almost no unit tests. A tax rounding bug was caught only by an E2E test, and it took an hour to find the line. What is the best long-term fix?
choices: Add more E2E tests around the checkout page
Run the E2E suite twice to make sure failures are real
Add unit tests for the tax calculation and keep E2E for critical journeys
Replace all automated tests with a manual QA checklist
questions.explanation: Logic like tax rounding belongs under fast unit tests that name the broken case directly. Keep a few E2E tests for the journeys that must work end to end. More E2E tests would make the slow, hard-to-debug part bigger.

questions.question: Put the steps of this arrange-act-assert test in order.
items: Create a fake clock set to 2026-03-01 09:00
Create an Account with balance 100 that uses the fake clock
Assert the balance is 70 and the last transaction time is 09:00
questions.explanation: Arrange builds everything the code needs (the clock, then the account that depends on it), act performs the single action, and assert checks the outcome.

questions.question: This test passes, yet apply_tax(200, 8) returns 360.0 instead of 216.0. What is wrong with the test?
choices: It should use pytest.approx because the result is a float
The arrange step must be split over two lines
It recomputes the expected value with the same buggy formula; assert the literal 216.0
Tests cannot assign two variables on one line
questions.explanation: Copying the formula into the test means the test agrees with whatever the code does, bug included. Work the answer out by hand (200 plus 8% is 216) and assert that literal. pytest.approx helps with tiny float errors, not a factor-of-ten bug.

questions.question: `test_delete_user` passes only when `test_create_user` runs before it. Which property of a good test is broken?
choices: Speed
Independence
Self-checking
Timeliness
questions.explanation: Each test should set up its own data and pass alone or in any order. Relying on another test's leftovers makes failures depend on ordering, not on the code.

questions.question: Why should each test check one behavior instead of bundling many unrelated asserts?
questions.answer: A test stops at its first failed assert, so later checks are hidden, and one name cannot describe many behaviors. Separate tests report every failure and say exactly which promise broke.
questions.explanation: Several asserts about one outcome are fine. Ten asserts about ten behaviors turn one red line in CI into a guessing game.

questions.question: Complete the pytest test so it passes only if withdraw raises ValueError.
questions.code:
import pytest
from accounts import withdraw

def test_withdrawing_more_than_balance_raises():
    with _____(ValueError):
        withdraw(balance=50, amount=80)
choices: pytest.throws
self.assertRaises
pytest.raises
pytest.catch
questions.explanation: pytest.raises is a context manager that fails the test unless the block raises the given exception. self.assertRaises is the unittest version and only exists on a TestCase class; pytest has no throws or catch helpers.

questions.question: Complete the Vitest test so it checks that parseAge throws for a negative age.
choices: parseAge(-1)
() => parseAge(-1)
parseAge
await parseAge(-1)
questions.explanation: toThrow needs a function it can call inside its own try block. parseAge(-1) runs before expect, so the error escapes and crashes the test. Passing bare parseAge would call it with no argument, which tests something else.

questions.question: uniqueSorted really returns [1, 2, 3], but this test fails. Why?
choices: Vitest compares arrays in reverse order
The test must be wrapped in a describe block
The test needs to be async because arrays are compared lazily
toBe checks identity with Object.is, and the result is a different array; use toEqual
questions.explanation: The function builds a new array, and the literal [1, 2, 3] is another new array. They have equal contents but are not the same object, so Object.is is false. toEqual compares contents.

questions.question: Run only the pytest tests whose names contain `coupon`.
questions.explanation: -k selects tests by a keyword expression matched against test names. It is the fastest way to rerun the handful of tests you are working on.

questions.question: By default pytest collects test files named `*_test.py` and one other pattern. Type that other pattern.
questions.explanation: pytest looks for test_*.py or *_test.py files, then for functions whose names start with test. A file named tests_cart.py or cart_tests.py is silently skipped.

questions.question: How does pytest run and report this test?
choices: As three separate tests, one per row, each passing or failing on its own
As one test that stops at the first failing row
As one test that passes only if every row passes, with no per-row detail
As three tests that must run in parallel
questions.explanation: parametrize generates one test per row, with ids such as test_factorial[5-120]. If one row fails, the others still run and report separately, which tells you exactly which input broke.

questions.question: Does test_cart_starts_empty pass when test_add_item runs first?
choices: No: the fixture returns the same Cart to every test in the file
Only if pytest happens to run the tests in alphabetical order
No: fixtures run once per session unless you say otherwise
Yes: a fixture's default scope is function, so each test gets a fresh Cart
questions.explanation: Fixtures default to function scope: pytest calls cart() again for every test that asks for it. You only share an instance across tests if you ask for a wider scope such as scope="module", which is also how leaked state and order dependence creep in.

questions.question: A coupon applies to orders with 3 to 10 items, inclusive. Which set of item counts tests the boundaries best?
choices: 3 and 10 only
0 and 100
questions.explanation: Each boundary needs its edge and the neighbor on the other side: 2 and 3 for the lower limit, 10 and 11 for the upper. Testing only 3 and 10 would miss a rule that wrongly accepts 2 or 11.

questions.question: Both asserts pass. Which edge case exposes a bug in last_n?
questions.code:
def last_n(items, n):
    """Return the last n items."""
    return items[-n:]

assert last_n([1, 2, 3, 4], 2) == [3, 4]
assert last_n([1, 2, 3], 3) == [1, 2, 3]
choices: An empty list raises IndexError
n = 0 returns the whole list, because items[-0:] is items[0:]
n larger than the list raises IndexError
Negative indexes do not work on lists
questions.explanation: -0 is just 0, so the slice becomes items[0:], the entire list, when the caller asked for nothing. Slicing never raises IndexError, so the empty-list and large-n cases quietly return sensible results.

questions.question: You are testing `average(numbers)`. Which inputs are worth a separate test?
choices: An empty list
A list with a single number
A list containing negative numbers
[2, 4, 6] and then also [4, 6, 8]
Floats such as [0.1, 0.2]
questions.explanation: Empty (division by zero), single element, negatives and floats each probe a different way the code can fail. [2, 4, 6] and [4, 6, 8] come from the same partition of ordinary positive integers, so the second adds nothing.

questions.question: A password must be 8 to 64 characters long. Using boundary value analysis, what is the shortest length above the limit that should be rejected? Type the number.
questions.explanation: The upper boundary is 64 (the last valid length), so you test 64 and its invalid neighbor 65. On the lower side you would test 8 and 7.

questions.question: Match each test double to what it does.

pairs.right: Returns a fixed exchange rate of 1.10 every time it is asked
Lets you assert send_email was called once with ana@example.com
An in-memory dictionary that stores and returns users like the real repository
Fills a required parameter but is never actually used

questions.explanation: Stubs feed canned answers in, mocks let you verify calls going out, fakes are working lightweight implementations, and dummies only satisfy a function signature.

questions.question: The real email is still sent and the assertion fails. Why?
questions.code:
# billing.py
from emails import send_email

def charge(customer):
    ...
    send_email(customer.email, "Receipt")

# test_billing.py
from unittest.mock import patch
import billing

def test_charge_sends_receipt():
    customer = make_customer()
    with patch("emails.send_email") as fake_send:
        billing.charge(customer)
    fake_send.assert_called_once()
choices: billing imported send_email into its own namespace, so patch billing.send_email instead
patch only works as a decorator, never as a context manager
assert_called_once requires the expected arguments
Mocks can replace classes but not plain functions
questions.explanation: from emails import send_email copies the reference into billing when the module loads. Patching emails.send_email later changes the name in emails, but billing still calls its own copy. Patch the name where it is looked up: billing.send_email.

questions.question: A test mocks the repository, cache, logger and formatter and asserts the exact order of seven calls. A teammate refactors to check the cache first; the output is identical, and the test fails. What is the real problem?
choices: The test checks implementation details instead of behavior, so it is brittle
The refactor must have introduced a bug
Mocks should always be replaced with stubs
The test needs an extra mock for the cache
questions.explanation: If behavior is unchanged and a test fails, the test was coupled to how the code works. Assert on outcomes (the returned value, the saved row) and keep doubles for real boundaries.

questions.question: Give a rule of thumb for what to replace with test doubles in unit tests and what to leave real.
questions.answer: Replace things at the edge of your system that are slow, nondeterministic or have side effects: network calls, payment and email providers, the clock, randomness. Use real objects or simple fakes for your own code inside that edge, and cover each boundary with a few integration tests.
questions.explanation: Doubles at the boundary keep tests fast and deterministic without hiding bugs in your own logic. Doubles deep inside your own code make tests mirror the implementation.

questions.question: Complete the line so the test can check how many times send was called.
questions.code:
import { it, expect, vi } from 'vitest'
import { notifyOverdue } from './notify.js'

it('sends one reminder per overdue invoice', () => {
  const send = _____
  notifyOverdue([{ id: 1, overdue: true }, { id: 2, overdue: false }], send)
  expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
})
choices: vi.mock()
vi.fn()
vi.spyOn()
questions.explanation: vi.fn() creates a mock function that records every call, which toHaveBeenCalledTimes reads. A plain arrow function records nothing, vi.mock replaces a whole module by path, and vi.spyOn needs an object and a method name to wrap.

questions.question: Put one lap of the TDD loop in order.
items: Write a small test for the next behavior
Run it and watch it fail
Write the simplest code that makes it pass
Run the tests and see them all pass
Refactor while keeping the tests green
questions.explanation: Red (a failing test), green (just enough code), then refactor with the safety net in place. Then start the next lap.

questions.question: A bug report says users named O'Brien cannot sign up. Working test-first, what is your first step?
choices: Fix the quoting in the signup handler, then deploy
Write a test that signs up O'Brien, run it and watch it fail
Add logging in production to catch the next occurrence
Write tests for every other field on the form first
questions.explanation: Reproducing the bug as a failing test proves you understand it, tells you when the fix works, and stays in the suite as a regression test so the bug cannot quietly return.

questions.question: In the green step you write `return 120` to pass `test_factorial_of_5`. Is that acceptable in TDD?
choices: No: the green step must always contain the final algorithm
No: hard-coded values make tests fail in CI
Yes, and you can stop there because the test passes
Yes, as a step: the next test, such as factorial of 3, forces a general solution
questions.explanation: Green means the simplest code that passes. A fake answer is fine for one lap, because the next test cannot pass with it and pushes you toward the real algorithm. Stopping there would leave the behavior untested beyond one value.

questions.question: This test reports 100% line and branch coverage for shipping. What is wrong with it?
choices: Coverage tools cannot measure if statements
Calling the function twice double-counts coverage
Nothing is asserted, so it passes even if shipping returns wrong values
It needs a call with exactly 50 before coverage can reach 100%
questions.explanation: Both branches ran, so coverage is complete, but the test never checks a result. Change return 0 to return 99 and it still passes. Coverage measures execution, not verification.

questions.question: Which of these commonly make a test flaky?
choices: Using time.sleep to wait for a background job
Sharing a module-level cache between tests
Calling a real third-party API from CI
Asserting a literal expected value
Depending on today's date
questions.explanation: Sleeps, shared state, external services and the real clock all vary from run to run. Asserting a literal value is deterministic, and it is good practice.

questions.question: This test fails about once in twenty CI runs. What is the best fix?
questions.code:
def test_report_job_finishes():
    start_report_job()
    time.sleep(2)
    assert report_status() == "done"
choices: Raise the sleep to 10 seconds
Set it to retry three times automatically and move on
Poll the status until done or a timeout, or run the job synchronously in tests
Remove the assert so the test always passes
questions.explanation: The test guesses how long the job takes. Waiting for the actual condition (with a generous timeout), or making the job synchronous in tests, removes the race. A longer sleep slows every run and can still lose on a busy machine; automatic retries hide the problem.

questions.question: What is the name for a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code?
questions.explanation: Flaky tests erode trust: people start rerunning red builds until they turn green, and real failures slip through.
